query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a dense alumina-based coating by high-temperature CVD or plasma-spraying onto boride-based components will significantly reduce their corrosion rate in molten aluminum compared to uncoated boride substrates.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based substrate (e.g., TiB2-containing composite) without a protective coating
generation.intervention: Deposit a uniform alumina-based ceramic layer using high-temperature CVD or plasma-spray methods
generation.conditions: Hot-dip aluminum-plating environment at 650–750 °C, under typical industrial atmosphere
generation.structural_mediator: A tightly adherent and crack-free alumina layer that impedes direct contact between molten aluminum and the boride substrate
generation.mechanism: The alumina coating forms a stable, low-solubility oxide barrier in molten aluminum, reducing interfacial reactions and inhibiting corrosive attack on the underlying boride material
generation.predicted_outcome: Corrosion rates in molten aluminum will decrease by at least 20–40% relative to an uncoated boride baseline, extending component service life
generation.baseline: Identical boride-based components operating under the same environmental conditions without any protective coating
generation.boundary: Effectiveness depends on achieving a dense, defect-free alumina coating; extremely high temperatures above ~750 °C or significant mechanical damage may impair the coating’s protective function
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvements depend on coating thickness and uniformity, and the molten aluminum composition; further testing is needed for quantitative validation in varied industrial conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based specimens. Coat one set with a uniform alumina film via high-temperature CVD or plasma-spraying. Expose both coated and uncoated sets to molten aluminum at 700 °C for a fixed duration, such as 200 hours, under identical process conditions.
measurements: Mass change and cross-sectional characterization to examine the extent of boride substrate dissolution
Elemental mapping (e.g., SEM-EDS) of cross-sections to identify aluminum infiltration or reaction zones
Microscopic inspection of the coating integrity to detect cracking or delamination
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens exhibit similar or greater mass loss and evidence of substrate dissolution compared to the uncoated controls, or if the alumina film does not reduce corrosion after 200 hours under these conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, a reinforced layer was prepared on the surface of HEA by powder-pack boriding and focused on the effect of temperature and duration on the boronizing of CoCrFeNiMn HEA. The boronized samples were characterized using various methods. Furthermore, the properties of boronized CoCrFeNiMn alloys and diffusion behavior were investigated. This study could provide a reference for high hardness and high wear resistance HEA that could be used in a variety of industrial applications, such as the mold and crucible used in the cast aluminum industry [,], because the borides formed on the surface have high hardness, excellent corrosion resistance, and wear resistance [,], which allow HEA to be applied in special environments to increase service life.

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr2O3), alumina (Al2O3) or silica (SiO2) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation. However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components,. The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

chosen.lever: Apply a protective alumina-based coating to the boride surface
chosen.technique: High-temperature CVD or plasma-spray ceramic deposition
chosen.why: Surface or interface engineering is a well-established route to reduce the direct reaction of molten aluminum with the substrate, providing robust, protective oxide layers that limit the component’s dissolution or degradation. Deposition methods such as high-temperature CVD or plasma-spraying are standard practices in the materials field and allow for a controlled, dense, and stable alumina film.
